flagship.headline: Dylan premieres A Hard Rain's a-Gonna Fall at Carnegie Hall
flagship.summary_line_1: Twenty-one-year-old Bob Dylan stepped onto the Carnegie Hall stage on September 22, 1962, for a Pete Seeger-organized hootenanny and sang A Hard Rain's a-Gonna Fall in public for the first time, according to Dylan's own official site.
flagship.summary_line_2: Seeger later called it the song that would outlast everything else Dylan wrote, and its warning landed with real weight just weeks before the Cuban Missile Crisis made the lyric feel prophetic.

events.headline: The Band release their self-titled second album
events.summary_line_1: Capitol Records released The Band's self-titled second album, often called the Brown Album, on September 22, 1969, cut largely in a makeshift studio inside Sammy Davis Jr.'s rented Los Angeles pool house.
events.summary_line_2: Songs like The Night They Drove Old Dixie Down and Up on Cripple Creek turned Robbie Robertson's rustic storytelling into a blueprint for Americana that shaped Eric Clapton, George Harrison, and a generation of roots-minded rock musicians.

events.headline: The Music Scene premieres on ABC with Crosby, Stills, Nash and Young
events.summary_line_1: ABC's weekly variety series The Music Scene premiered on September 22, 1969, hosted by David Steinberg, and its debut episode put the freshly formed Crosby, Stills, Nash and Young on network television playing Down by the River.
events.summary_line_2: James Brown and Three Dog Night filled out the same hour, giving the short-lived show one of the strongest lineups network TV offered folk rock and soul audiences that year.

events.headline: BBC airs Louis Armstrong's Show of the Week special
events.summary_line_1: BBC Television broadcast Show of the Week: Louis Armstrong on September 22, 1968, built around a concert Armstrong and his All Stars had taped at the BBC's London studios that July.
events.summary_line_2: Armstrong reportedly wrote "For The Fans" on the tape box himself, and in 2024 Verve pulled the audio into the live album Louis in London, preserving what turned out to be one of his last great filmed performances.

events.headline: Janis Ian plays Carnegie Hall at 16
events.summary_line_1: Sixteen-year-old Janis Ian performed a solo concert at Carnegie Hall on September 22, 1967, according to Setlist.fm's dated listing for the show.
events.summary_line_2: The booking came on the heels of Society's Child, her controversial single about an interracial romance, and confirmed her as one of the era's most serious young singer-songwriters.

events.headline: Jim Reeves tops the UK chart from beyond the grave with Distant Drums
events.summary_line_1: Distant Drums by Jim Reeves reached number one on the UK Singles Chart on September 22, 1966, more than two years after the country singer died in a 1964 plane crash, according to the Official Charts Company.
events.summary_line_2: Producer Chet Atkins had passed on the Cindy Walker song when Reeves first brought it to him in 1961, then added new orchestral backing and released it posthumously, holding the top spot for five weeks.

events.headline: The Supremes begin recording I Hear a Symphony
events.summary_line_1: Diana Ross, Mary Wilson, and Florence Ballard opened session work on I Hear a Symphony at Motown's Hitsville U.S.A. Studio A on September 22, 1965, with additional tracking dates running through September 30.
events.summary_line_2: The Holland-Dozier-Holland production went on to sell more than two million copies and gave the Supremes their sixth number-one single on the Billboard Hot 100.

events.headline: Fiddler on the Roof opens on Broadway
events.summary_line_1: Fiddler on the Roof opened at Broadway's Imperial Theatre on September 22, 1964, with Zero Mostel starring as Tevye under Jerome Robbins' direction and choreography.
events.summary_line_2: Songs like Tradition and If I Were a Rich Man carried the show to a record 3,242 performances and nine Tony Awards, a run that held the title of longest-running Broadway musical for years.

events.headline: Frank Ifield yodels his way through The Ed Sullivan Show
events.summary_line_1: British-Australian singer Frank Ifield performed his UK number-one hit I'm Confessin' (That I Love You) live on The Ed Sullivan Show on September 22, 1963, sharing the bill with the vocal group the Dallas Boys.
events.summary_line_2: Ifield's trademark yodel break gave American prime-time audiences an early taste of Commonwealth pop-country crossover, right before the British Invasion bands behind him took over the same stage.

events.headline: Dylan premieres A Hard Rain's a-Gonna Fall at Carnegie Hall
events.summary_line_1: Twenty-one-year-old Bob Dylan stepped onto the Carnegie Hall stage on September 22, 1962, for a Pete Seeger-organized hootenanny and sang A Hard Rain's a-Gonna Fall in public for the first time, according to Dylan's own official site.
events.summary_line_2: Seeger later called it the song that would outlast everything else Dylan wrote, and its warning landed with real weight just weeks before the Cuban Missile Crisis made the lyric feel prophetic.

events.headline: Five Star Jubilee airs its final NBC broadcast
events.summary_line_1: Five Star Jubilee, the country music variety series hosted by Red Foley with Slim Wilson's Jubilee Band, aired its final NBC broadcast on September 22, 1961, closing out a run that began that March from the Landers Theatre in Springfield, Missouri.
events.summary_line_2: The show had been one of network television's earliest color broadcasts produced outside New York or Hollywood, carrying the same country talent pipeline that fed Ozark Jubilee before it.

events.headline: The Twist keeps its grip on the Billboard Hot 100
events.summary_line_1: Chubby Checker's The Twist held its Billboard Hot 100 number-one spot straight through September 22, 1960, the middle of the single week it topped the chart during its first run.
events.summary_line_2: The song returned to number one again in January 1962, making it the only single in Hot 100 history to top the chart during two separate, non-consecutive runs, a feat not matched again until Mariah Carey's All I Want for Christmas Is You decades later.
